title: Sin as slavery; Christ redeems into liberty and service of righteousness
source_text: XII. Praeterea de iis qui peccatis indulgent Scriptura loquitur tanquam peccati servis, & mancipiis vitiorum, qui duro quodam peccati dominio premuntur, & sub eo sunt quasi venundati. Omnis, inquit Christus, qui facit peccatum servus est peccati. Joan. 8. Et Petrus impios illos, in quos posteriore epistola invehitur, affirmat esse servos corruptionis, a quo enim quis superatus est, hujus, inquit, & servus est. Unde est quod dicitur Christus nos redimere ab iniquitate, quasi qui sub ea captivi essemus, & nos a foeda peccati servitute in libertatem vindicare. Peccatum, inquit Paulus, vobis non dominabitur; non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Rom. 6. Nam, ut ibidem docet, Vetus noster homo simul cum Christo crucifixus est, ut destruatur corpus peccati, ut ultra non serviamus peccato. Et sub finem illius capitis, Liberati, inquit, a peccato, facti estis servi justitiae.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, of those who indulge sins Scripture speaks as of servants of sin and bondslaves of vices, who are pressed by a hard dominion of sin and are under it as if sold. Everyone who commits sin, says Christ, is a servant of sin (John 8). And Peter affirms that those impious against whom he inveighs in the later epistle are servants of corruption; for by whatever one is overcome, of that he is also a servant. Hence it is that Christ is said to redeem us from iniquity, as those who were captive under it, and to claim us from foul slavery of sin into liberty. Sin shall not have dominion over you, says Paul; for you are not under law but under grace (Romans 6). For, as he teaches there, our old man was crucified together with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer serve sin. And toward the end of that chapter: Having been freed from sin, he says, you were made servants of righteousness.
pass_b_english: Scripture casts indulged sin as hard slavery (John 8; 2 Peter).
Christ redeems captives into liberty; under grace sin no longer masters—old man crucified, servants of righteousness (Romans 6).
